title: Oxidised jewellery: what it is and how to style it
description: Oxidised jewellery is metal darkened on purpose for an antique look. Learn how it is made, what it is made of, how to style it and how to keep it nice.
intro: Oxidised jewellery is metal that has been darkened on purpose to look old. The recessed parts of the design are left grey or black while the raised parts are polished, which makes patterns stand out and gives that rustic, tribal or vintage feel. It is the jhumka you wear with a cotton kurta, the chunky ring you wear with jeans, and it is one of the easiest styles to wear every day.

sections.heading: What 'oxidised' actually means
paragraphs: Silver and many base metals naturally darken when they react with air and sulphur over time. Oxidised jewellery speeds this up deliberately: the finished piece is treated with a chemical solution that darkens the surface, and then the high points are rubbed back to a lighter shine.
The result is contrast. A flat silver jhumka can look plain, but the same design oxidised shows every flower, bead and groove. That is why oxidised finishes are so common on heavily detailed designs.

sections.heading: What it is usually made of
paragraphs: Not all oxidised jewellery is silver. When you buy it, you are usually getting one of these:
list: Oxidised 925 sterling silver: real silver with a darkened finish. It costs more, but it can be cleaned and re-finished by a silversmith.
German silver: despite the name, it contains no silver. It is an alloy of copper, nickel and zinc with a silvery colour, widely used for affordable oxidised pieces.
White metal or other alloys: inexpensive, light and easy to cast into detailed shapes. Common in budget earrings and chokers.

sections.heading: A note for sensitive skin
paragraphs: Because German silver contains nickel and some alloys may too, people with nickel sensitivity sometimes react to cheaper oxidised jewellery, especially earrings. If your earlobes get itchy or red, look for pieces with hooks marked nickel-free, or choose 925 silver. If a reaction continues, check with a doctor rather than pushing through it.

sections.heading: How to style oxidised jewellery
paragraphs: The golden rule is one hero piece. Oxidised designs are already busy with detail, so a big choker plus big jhumkas plus a stack of bangles can look heavy very quickly. Let the largest piece set the tone and keep everything else small.
Oxidised pieces love natural fabrics and earthy colours. They look most at home with cotton, khadi, linen, handloom and ikat, in shades like indigo, rust, mustard, olive, white and black.
list: Big oxidised jhumkas with a plain white or black kurta and kolhapuris, nothing else.
A layered oxidised choker with a handloom saree and a sleeveless blouse.
A statement ring and a few thin bangles with a denim shirt and jeans for college or a weekend.
Long oxidised earrings with an indigo dress for a day out or a music event.
A single oxidised nose pin or toe ring for a subtle boho touch.

sections.heading: What to check before buying
paragraphs: Oxidised jewellery is inexpensive, so it is tempting to buy without looking closely. A minute of checking saves disappointment:
list: The dark finish should sit evenly in the grooves, not in random patches.
Raised areas should be cleanly polished, so the design reads clearly from a distance.
Large earrings should feel light enough for a full day. Heavy alloy jhumkas can drag the earlobe.
Hooks and jump rings should be firmly closed, with no sharp edges that catch hair or fabric.
Ghungroo beads and hanging drops should be attached with closed loops, not just bent wire.

sections.heading: When to choose something else
paragraphs: Oxidised jewellery is casual by nature. For a wedding, a formal reception or a silk saree, it can look underdressed next to the fabric. That is when gold-toned Kundan, temple or AD pieces work better.

It also does not mix well with bright yellow gold-tone jewellery in the same look. Pick one metal story per outfit. If you love the silver tone but want something a little more polished for office or dinners, a plain [925 sterling silver pendant](/silver) on a fine chain bridges the gap nicely.

sections.heading: Caring for oxidised pieces
paragraphs: The biggest mistake is cleaning oxidised jewellery like ordinary silver. Silver dip and strong polish remove tarnish, and that includes the deliberate dark finish you paid for. Instead, wipe it gently with a soft dry cloth after wearing.

Keep pieces in separate zip pouches with the air pressed out, away from the bathroom. Avoid perfume and water contact. German silver and alloys can leave a greenish mark on skin with sweat, so wipe them down after a long day, particularly in summer. With this basic care, a good oxidised pair can last you many seasons.

faq.a: Sometimes. It can be 925 sterling silver, but much of it is German silver or other alloys. Check the description or ask the seller.

faq.q: Can oxidised jewellery be worn daily?
faq.a: Yes, it is one of the most casual, everyday-friendly styles. Keep it dry and wipe it after wearing so it lasts longer.

faq.q: Why does oxidised jewellery leave green marks?
faq.a: Copper in German silver and some alloys reacts with sweat and moisture, which can leave a green tint on skin.

faq.q: Can I clean oxidised jewellery with silver polish?
faq.a: Avoid it. Silver polish removes the darkened finish. A soft dry cloth is enough.
